title: To whom?
goal: Complete the six noun forms with the "to" form, use verbs that require it, and express possession the Roman way with est mihi.
bekal: make the singular and plural "to" form for the first two groups
say "I have" in two ways: *habeo* and *est mihi*

dialogs.title: Colloquium — Epistula ad avum
dialogs.intro: Marcus is writing a letter to his grandfather in Sicily. Iulia notices something unfair.

lines.speaker: Iulia:
lines.id: Who are you writing a letter to, Marcus?

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.text: Avo scribo. Avus in Sicilia habitat.
lines.id: To Grandpa. Grandpa lives in Sicily.
lines.literal: grandfather-to write-I. grandfather in Sicily-in live-he.

lines.speaker: Iulia:
lines.id: And what are you telling Grandpa?

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.text: Avo de schola narro. Et de dono quoque.
lines.id: I'm telling Grandpa about school. And about a present too.
lines.literal: grandfather-to about school-about tell-I. and about gift-about also.

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.text: Ita! Avus mihi semper dona mittit.
lines.id: Yes! Grandpa always sends me presents.
lines.literal: yes! grandfather me-to always gift-pl-obj send-he.

lines.speaker: Iulia:
lines.text: Et mihi? Avus mihi numquam dona mittit!
lines.id: What about me? Grandpa never sends me presents!
lines.literal: and me-to? grandfather me-to never gift-pl-obj send-he!

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.text: Tu avo non scribis, Iulia! Ergo avus tibi non mittit.
lines.id: You don't write to Grandpa, Iulia! So Grandpa doesn't send you anything.
lines.literal: you grandfather-to not write-you, Iulia! so grandfather you-to not send-he.

lines.speaker: Iulia:
lines.text: Vera dicis. Hodie avo et aviae scribo.
lines.id: That's true. Today I'll write to Grandpa and Grandma.
lines.literal: true-pl-neut-obj say-you. today grandfather-to and grandmother-to write-I.

lines.speaker: Cornelia:
lines.text: Bene, filia. Litterae amicis gaudium dant.
lines.id: Good, daughter. Letters bring joy to friends.
lines.literal: well, daughter-call. letter-pl friend-pl-to joy-obj give-they.

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.id: Mom, do you have a pen?

lines.speaker: Cornelia:
lines.text: Est mihi stilus, sed non est mihi patientia!
lines.id: I have a pen, but I don't have the patience!
lines.literal: is-it me-to pen, but not is-it me-to patience!

notes: **Cui? — "to whom?"** This is the "to" form of *quis*. Latin uses one form for what English splits into "to" and "for". So *avo scribo* can be translated "I'm writing to Grandpa" or "I'm writing for Grandpa" — and both are right.

**Est mihi stilus — the Roman way to say "I have".** Literally "there is a pen to me". Latin does have *habeo*, but this pattern is older and sounds more natural for things a person simply has. Notice that the thing owned becomes the **subject**, not the object: *stilus*, not *stilum*.

**Avo, aviae, amicis — three "to" endings in one dialogue.** Group two uses *-o*, group one uses *-ae*, and the plural of both uses *-is*. The same *-is* ending is also used for the "with/in" form, so one form does two jobs — the preposition tells them apart.

**Vera dicis — a neuter plural adjective used as a noun.** *Vera* means "true things", so *vera dicis* is "you're saying true things", that is, "you're right". It's the pattern you've already seen in *multa* and *cetera*.

blocks.text: With the "to" form, the noun table for groups one and two is now complete. There will be no new forms until the end of the course; all that's left are other noun groups with different endings.

Two new look-alikes appear, and it's best to notice them now. First, *puellae* can now mean three things: singular "of", plural subject, or singular "to". Second, *amicis* and *puellis* serve as both plural "to" and plural "with/in". Latin lives at peace with these twins because the sentence always gives clues: the verb, the preposition, and common sense.
There are many kinds of "giving" verbs, and they all follow the same pattern: the thing given takes the object form, the receiver takes the "to" form.

rows: I give a gift to a friend.
I send a letter to Grandpa.
She tells the children a story.
I show the house to my friends.

blocks.text: There's also a group of verbs that in English seem to take an ordinary object, but in Latin require the "to" form. The group is small, and it's best learned as a whole.

head: Latin
Meaning
Example
rows: Fabula **mihi** placet. — I like the story.

blocks.text: *Placet* is worth learning whole: *mihi placet* is the Latin way to say "I like it", literally "it pleases me". Spanish and Italian inherited this way of thinking with *me gusta* and *mi piace*.

head: Job
Example
Translation
rows: I give the book to the girl.
I'm making dinner for the children.
We learn not for school, but for life.

blocks.text: That last sentence — *non scholae sed vitae discimus* — is Seneca's complaint, turned around by later schoolmasters, and it's still carved on many school buildings in Europe. You can already read it word by word.

blocks.title: Two ways to say "have"
items: *Librum habeo.* — the owner is the subject, the thing is the object. This is the closest to English "I have a book".
*Mihi est liber.* — the thing is the subject, the owner takes the "to" form. This is the most Roman way, and the most common for qualities: *mihi est patientia* ("I have patience").
Both are correct. For things you hold, *habeo* is more natural; for qualities, relationships and names, *est mihi* is more natural: *nomen mihi est Marcus* — "my name is Marcus".
